ruling_text:

Agricultural and industrial users were reduced to reflect the need to preserve scarce water for immediate human welfare and system resilience, while environmental flows were temporarily deferred because no consensus package could secure a workable balance within the two negotiation rounds.

We note and commend any voluntary reductions or trades offered during negotiations as evidence of good-faith crisis management; such cooperation will be weighed favorably in future allocation decisions.

Today’s ruling prioritised life-sustaining and essential public services under extreme heat, with special weight given to hospitals, household use, and the minimum water needed to keep the power system stable and prevent cascading failures. Agriculture and industry were assigned reduced shares because, while important, they can absorb short-term curtailment more readily than health, domestic supply, or critical infrastructure, and environmental releases were necessarily deferred in light of the acute shortage.

We note the voluntary cooperation shown in negotiation, including the willingness of the Energy Utility and several other stakeholders to accept reductions and trade-offs to keep the system functioning. The Authority regards such good-faith crisis management as materially helpful and it will be weighed favourably in future allocation decisions.

Agriculture and environmental flows were reduced to reflect the need to protect immediate human welfare under emergency conditions, and industry/business use was suspended for the day because it was the most deferrable demand in this shortage.

We note that the final outcome followed two rounds of negotiation without consensus, requiring a formal ruling. Any stakeholders who accepted voluntary reductions or trades during the process demonstrated good-faith crisis management, and the Authority will take that cooperation into account favorably in future allocation decisions.
